title: A sequel to ‘The Art of Fielding’ gives it the old college try
text:
A sequel to ‘The Art of Fielding’ gives it the old college try
Chad Harbach’s first novel, “The Art of Fielding,” arrived in 2011 with a fanfare of publicity and a flurry of plaudits. Amid the hoopla, readers learned of the book’s checkered history. Harbach spent a decade writing it; it was turned down by umpteen literary gatekeepers; eventually, one plucky young agent took a chance on it, and a bidding war ensued. News of a high advance unleashed correspondingly high expectations. Could this debut live up to the ballyhoo surrounding it?
For the most part, it could and it did. Harbach’s novel, which went on to become a bestseller, was a big-hearted, multi-stranded affair that followed several characters in and around Westish College, memorably described as “that little school in the crook of the baseball glove that is Wisconsin.” The baseball analogy was apt. Harbach’s cast of strivers and dreamers included dazzling baseball shortstop Henry Skrimshander, his mentor Mike Schwartz, and Pella Affenlight, who made up a love triangle.
Now, 15 years later, Harbach returns with his second novel, one that can be read as both a sequel of sorts to its predecessor and a stand-alone work. In “The Brightness,” Harbach reprises the setting and reintroduces some of the characters from his debut. On this occasion, though, his focus is on female protagonists, specifically Pella. Long-awaited rather than much-hyped, the book offers a deft portrayal of women navigating young adulthood’s complexities.
In his sophomore novel “The Brightness,” Chad Harbach revisits the young adult students at Westish College.
It is 2015 and Pella, a former wild child once powered by impulsive energy and rebellious streaks, has grown up and settled down. She has recently graduated from Westish. Her disastrous first marriage is behind her. She’s now engaged to Mike, who, after hanging up his baseball glove, took on a job as a coach and assistant athletic director at the college. Pella is currently dividing her time between helping her fiancé study for the law school admissions test and planning her writer friend Owen’s destination wedding off the coast of Rhode Island. But her own future plans are less certain. She is rudderless, unsure which career path to take. Compounding this lack of direction is a nagging worry that her best friend, Irma Friske, is acting strange and becoming distant.
Pella has good cause for concern. Irma, a gifted scholarship student, has secretly joined forces with two other, more outgoing college seniors, Pammy Chang and the dangerously alluring Dahlia Breughel. The trio form the Witches of Westish. At a party, they launch an audacious project they have devised, one which results in two football players waking up the next morning with provocative words written on their foreheads. The stunt highlights the plight of sexual assault on college campuses.
A video of the deeds goes viral. Word spreads, first around Westish and then across the country. It sparks debate: Was this performance art or a jock-orchestrated prank? Or might it be a more impassioned, politically motivated project designed to raise awareness? The group’s exploits rouse the ire of a cable news host who brands the women “harpies with Sharpies.” But they also garner support from thousands of commenters on the Brightness, an influential website “for women talking to women,” many of whom praise the Witches and come to believe that Westish is home to “a grand inland battle between male privilege and female courage.”
While Mike comes under fire for his handling of the situation, and the college scrambles to staunch bad publicity and track down the “perpetrators,” Pella celebrates Owen’s wedding day on Block Island. But certain guests cramp her style. Katrina, an erstwhile nemesis from her school days, discomfits her by showing only kindness rather than animosity. Irma’s unexpected arrival confirms Pella’s belief that she is out to “annex” her friends. And then there is the captivating presence of a handsome and flirtatious accountant called Nicholas.
Over the course of the wedding weekend, Pella endures her unfair share of arguments, betrayals, and hostile truths. Instead of returning home, she heads to New York City where, in self-imposed exile, she attempts to work out what she truly wants and how she can go about getting it.
Weighing in at well over 600 pages, this is a big beast of a novel. Perhaps inevitably, the narrative sags in places due to tangential flashbacks and extended episodes and exchanges in which every detail, action, gesture, and impulse are recorded. Harbach’s grand set piece on Block Island packs a punch but only after a considerable buildup.
“This wedding was a novel that, though long in the making, would take one night to read,” Pella says. Two or three nights would be more realistic.
However, during the book’s more streamlined scenes, Harbach triumphs on various levels. He explores diverse topics from marital strife to literary merit to gender inequality. The author delivers finely wrought drama and nuanced character studies. He ensures we root for both Pella and Irma during challenges in their messy lives and tangled relationships.
In Harbach’s hands, Pella emerges as a compellingly flawed creation. “You’re afraid of your desires and your ambitions,” Irma tells her. “You’re afraid that if you let them out of the house, they’ll eat the whole world.”
“The Brightness” brilliantly illuminates those hopes, loves, and fears.
